(A) is the only statement that does not agree with what is known about the virus.

Why the others are acceptable

• (B)  Several independent studies on SARS-CoV and, more recently, on SARS-CoV-2 show that ORF3a activates/cleaves caspase-8 while leaving the level of Bcl-2 essentially unchanged.  Caspase-8 belongs to the death-receptor (extrinsic) pathway, whereas Bcl-2 regulates the mitochondrial (intrinsic) pathway, so the conclusion drawn in the statement is consistent with the experimental data.

• (C)  Single-molecule‐force spectroscopy has revealed that frameshift-stimulating pseudoknots able to adopt multiple alternative folds (two or more) give higher –1 PRF efficiencies, and both the SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 pseudoknots have been shown to interchange between two dominant pseudoknotted conformers under tension, in line with that observation.

• (D)  In coronaviruses the ribosome can shift back by one nucleotide at the slippery sequence just upstream of a stimulatory pseudoknot, producing the short pp1a and the longer pp1ab polyproteins encoded at the 5´ end.  The SARS-CoV-2 –1 PRF signal is almost identical in sequence and structure to that of SARS-CoV, so the statement is accurate.

Why (A) is wrong

Nsp14’s N-terminal domain is a 3′→5′ exoribonuclease (ExoN) whose activity is strongly stimulated by its co-factor nsp10; together they form a proofreading heterodimer that excises mis-incorporated ribonucleotides from the nascent RNA strand.  In other words, the complex catalyses the breakdown (removal) of mismatched bases in the double-stranded replication intermediate; it does not “prevent the breakdown of dsRNA.”  The statement therefore mis-describes the action of the nsp10/nsp14 complex.

Answer: A
